common_name: Bloomsdale Long Standing Spinach (Heirloom Savoy Spinach)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, 4-6 weeks before the last frost, in rows about a foot apart.

directions: Direct sow seed a half inch deep into cool, moist soil as soon as the ground can be worked, thinning seedlings to a few inches apart once true leaves appear. This selection is one of the oldest named spinach types still grown today, prized for its heavily crinkled, dark green savoy leaves and slower tendency to bolt compared with smooth-leaf types. It tolerates light frost and often tastes sweetest after a cold snap, making it a dependable choice for both early spring and fall sowings.

common_name: Winter Bloomsdale Spinach (Cold-Hardy Overwintering Savoy Spinach)

planting.note: Sow 4-6 weeks before the first hard fall frost so plants are established but not overly mature going into winter.

directions: Sow directly in late summer or early fall so seedlings size up before short days and cold arrive, then protect with a low tunnel or thick mulch through the coldest months for an early spring harvest. This vigorous savoy-leaf hybrid was bred specifically for exceptional cold tolerance and holds its dark, crinkled foliage through hard freezes better than standard Bloomsdale types. Many growers value it as one of the most reliable spinach selections for season extension in cold climates.

subcategory: baby-leaf hybrid spinach with red veining

planting.note: Direct sow thickly in wide bands 2-4 weeks before the last frost for a quick baby-leaf harvest.

directions: Broadcast or row sow seed thickly and shallowly, keeping the bed consistently moist for even germination, then cut leaves with scissors once they reach salad size. This smooth, arrow-shaped hybrid is distinguished by its bright pink-red midribs and veins running through tender green leaves, adding color and a mild, slightly sweet flavor to fresh salad mixes. It resists bolting better than many baby-leaf types and regrows readily for repeat cuttings.

common_name: Argentata Swiss Chard (Silver Ribbed Italian Heirloom Chard)

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date, or a bit earlier under cover, spacing seed clusters several inches apart.

directions: Sow seed clusters directly into fertile soil, thinning to one seedling per cluster once plants have a couple of true leaves, and keep beds evenly watered through summer heat. This old Italian type produces broad, dull green savoyed leaves atop wide, flat, silvery-white ribs that many cooks prize for braising separately from the greens. It is notably heat tolerant and slow to bolt, allowing continuous cut-and-come-again harvest well into the warm months.

common_name: Vulcan Swiss Chard (Brilliant Red-Stemmed French Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date and thin seedlings once established; plants tolerate light frost in fall.

directions: Direct sow into loose, fertile soil and thin seedlings to their final spacing, watering consistently to keep stalks tender and prevent bitterness. This French heirloom is grown chiefly for its glossy, deep crimson stalks and veins that hold their vivid color even after cooking, contrasting with dark green, slightly savoyed leaves. It is a dependable cut-and-come-again green that keeps producing new leaves from the crown for months.

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date, thinning to final spacing as seedlings develop true leaves.

directions: Sow directly and thin plants to stand several inches apart, keeping soil evenly moist to encourage broad, tender leaves. Unlike multicolor chard blends, this selection breeds true for solid golden-yellow stalks and veins beneath crumpled dark green leaves, giving a uniform look for market bunching. Its flavor is mild and slightly sweeter than red-stemmed types, and it holds up well as both a baby green and a mature cooking chard.

common_name: Starbor Kale (Compact Dwarf Curly Hybrid Kale)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant 4-6 weeks before the last frost; also sow in mid to late summer for a fall crop.

directions: Sow seed a half inch deep and thin or transplant to final spacing, side-dressing with compost as plants size up. This compact, uniform hybrid produces tightly curled, dark blue-green leaves on short stems, making it well suited to close spacing and mechanical or hand bunch harvesting. Its short, dense habit and slow bolting have made it a standard choice for market growers wanting a tidy, consistent curly kale.

common_name: Ripbor Kale (Tall Frilly Red-Purple Hybrid Curly Kale)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant 4-6 weeks before the last frost, or sow in summer for a fall and winter harvest.

directions: Direct sow or start indoors and transplant, giving plants ample room to reach their full upright height, and harvest lower leaves first as the plant continues growing from the top. This hybrid was bred as a red-purple counterpart to the popular green curly hybrids, with tightly ruffled maroon-purple leaves on tall, sturdy stems. Cold exposure deepens its color and sweetens its flavor, and its height makes it a striking option for both the vegetable garden and cut-foliage use.

common_name: Groninger Blue Kale (Dutch Heirloom Feathery Kale)

planting.note: Sow in mid to late summer, 10-14 weeks before the first fall frost, for a fall and winter harvest after cold sweetens the leaves.

directions: Direct sow in mid-summer and thin to wide final spacing so plants can develop their large, sprawling frames before winter sets in. This traditional Dutch farmhouse kale, long grown around the province of Groningen, produces finely divided, feathery blue-green leaves on tall stems and was historically a winter storage vegetable harvested straight from the frozen garden. Repeated frost exposure noticeably mellows its flavor, and the plant continues producing new leaves from the top through much of the winter.

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before the last frost, or later in summer for a fall crop; leaves can be cut young or left to mature.

directions: Direct sow shallowly into fertile soil and thin seedlings as they grow, cutting outer leaves for continuous harvest or letting plants reach full size. This traditional Ethiopian selection produces large, smooth, paddle-shaped blue-green leaves with a sharper, more pungent bite than common mustard greens, and it is a staple ingredient in Ethiopian gomen dishes. It tolerates both heat and cool weather better than many mustards, giving it a longer harvest window through the season.

common_name: Fordhook Fancy Mustard (Curled Heirloom Mustard Green)

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before the last frost, or in late summer for a fall crop; harvest outer leaves young for the mildest flavor.

directions: Direct sow shallowly and thin seedlings to stand several inches apart, harvesting outer leaves regularly to keep the plant productive. This old American selection, once distributed under the Fordhook name, forms dense rosettes of tightly curled, ruffled bright green leaves with a peppery mustard bite that mellows when cooked. Its frilly texture makes it a distinctive addition to mixed braising greens, and it tends to hold in the garden a bit longer than plain-leaf mustards before bolting.
